source.title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
source.authors: Andrew Lee; Xiaoyan Bai; Itamar Hagay Pres; Martin Wattenberg; Jonathan K. Kummerfeld; R. Mihalcea

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies toxicity reduction in GPT2-medium, not refusal or the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. Its discussion of jailbreaks is about toxicity alignment and does not test the listed refusal claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports interventions on toxicity-oriented vectors and measures toxic generation, but it does not measure refusal of harmful or harmless user requests, or test the refusal direction described in the claim. These related toxicity results are recorded with versions ["none"]. It does not test direction addition or a weight-edit method for removing refusals.
record.test_reason: The study examines toxicity vectors and DPO in GPT2-medium, a pre-trained non-chat model. It measures toxic generation, not refusal of harmful or harmless requests. It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. Its jailbreak discussion is a conjecture about toxicity alignment and does not test any version. It predates the original (2024) and is cited as related background; the recorded relation and tranche are correct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. DPO leaves the toxic MLP vectors intact and learns a small distributed offset that steers the residual stream away from their activation regions. Scaling a few toxic key vectors undoes the alignment. The authors frame this as a mechanistic case study of why alignment can be jailbroken.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a toxicity probe and identifies toxic MLP value vectors, then subtracts selected vectors from the last-layer residual stream. It does not find a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction or test refusal ablation/addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported toxicity intervention scale is chosen to make perplexity comparable to the post-DPO model. The seven-key-vector scaling result uses vectors selected by cosine similarity to WToxic.

fits_no_version.finding: Subtracting toxicity probe, MLP value, or SVD vectors from GPT2's last-layer residual stream cuts toxicity from 0.453 to 0.245–0.305, with perplexity rising from 21.7 to about 23.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toxicity-linked residual directions in pre-trained LMs causally mediate toxic generation.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO barely changes weights (cosine >0.99) and learns a distributed offset that bypasses toxic MLP regions. Scaling 7 toxic key vectors by 10x restores toxicity to 0.458 with unchanged perplexity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference alignment suppresses an undesired behaviour by bypassing its circuitry rather than removing it, so the behaviour can be cheaply re-enabled.

record.problems: All experiments use GPT2-medium and focus on toxicity rather than refusal. Perplexity and Wikipedia-continuation F1 are limited proxies for preserved capability. The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the reported table results.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results were reported. The rows retain the tabled toxicity, perplexity, and F1 results for the toxicity-vector interventions, DPO, and key-vector scaling, plus the described activation drop in Figure 2. Other figure-only geometry and parameter-shift plots are not separately recorded because they do not measure refusal or a claim-version outcome.

untested.parts: All: no refusal direction, no ablation or addition effects on refusal.
All: no weight edit removing refusal in released models.
All: the jailbreak link is conjectured only, for toxicity, with no direction-suppression test.
All. The KL-divergence role in distributed versus localized changes is only hypothesized, and for toxicity.

record.verdict_notes: This is toxicity in GPT2-medium, not refusal, and it predates the original source. It is conceptually adjacent to V2 and V3 (alignment as bypass, cheap un-alignment), but no row measures refusal. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Refusal direction discovery, ablation effects on refusal, adding the direction, and effects on other abilities in safety-trained chat models.
Weight-edit removal of refusal in released models.
Whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or training against its ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal is represented by an affine space, cone, or multiple directions.
Separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Whether training choices decide whether a removable refusal direction exists.
